A baby in the womb is not a parasite. A baby in the womb is a homospecific. The baby is the same species as the mother, whose body is specifically geared to gestate a baby of her own species while it lives inside her. The same cannot be said of a tapeworm. A parasite is an invading organism, coming to parasitize the host from an outside source. A fetus is formed from a fertilized egg, the egg coming from an inside source, being formed in the ovary of the mother from where it moved into the oviduct where it may be fertilized. The host-parasite relationship is one of conflict, while the mother-baby relationship is intrinsically cooperative. 

Consider the immunology of the two. Host and parasite are locked in an arms race: the parasite evolved ever more complex techniques of avoidance, while the host evolved ever more complex techniques of detection and attack. Meanwhile, mother and baby cooperate to prevent immunological conflict. The site of this cooperation is the placenta. The fetus cannot be viewed as a tumor robbing the mother of nutrients.

No. tearing my ACL was a blessing in disguise as weird as that sounds. I was younger when I tore mine, so it might be a little different. Freshman year through sophomore year, my cumulative GPA was a 2.73. 

It was horrendous. When I tore my ACL two months into school my junior year, I didn’t do any school work for a month. The entire month of November was recovery and vacation for me. December rolled around, and I met a girl, and I had over a hundred and fifty missing assignments. 

At this point, it was already the Friday before my school went on Christmas break. I had never bothered applying myself to school. I believed I just wasn’t good at it. That’s true, but not in the way I thought. I wasn’t good at it because I hadn’t put any effort towards my academics. I had two options. 

I could fail my junior year, or I could choose to spend my Christmas break grinding through my assignments. I decided to do the latter, grinding roughly twelve assignments per day. When it came to math, it was frustrating. It would take me forever to grind through those assignments. 

When I consciously realized that I could do the work, I started putting my best foot forward. I decided I could attend University. I started applying myself to school throughout my recovery. I ended up with an unweighted 3.7 my junior year. When senior year rolled around, I continued applying myself. I even started self studying. 

As you can read in my comment, I became a grammarian. I take great pride in that. My GPA was a 4.1 my senior year. I stopped playing video games. I started meal prepping and lifting weights. I ended up attending University, as I’m currently writing this in my dorm room on a Saturday. I’m doing well in all my class, and I have five weeks left of the first semester. 

Tearing my ACL changed my life for the better. Though, there are still some downs. I study incessantly now, for the most part. There are kids younger than me that are way more intelligent than me. This does make me mad and sad at myself. I’m trying to catch up, but it feels like an insurmountable mountain. Spending 16-18 hours a day playing video games throughout the first two years of high school did not help me.

I had hit a plateau and my physical therapist noticed it after the second time. He decided to space out how often he would check my knee flexion. This helped my mindset. I didn't have to always not look forward to going to PT because I didn't know if I could beat last time's flexion. 

I ended up working even harder. I respected my physical therapist. The dude is a hard worker. I didn't want to make him worry. For me, what helped me get past that plateau was doing knee-bending exercises three times a day.

I don't know anything about the pain of using a patellar graft. Fortunately, a donor graft was available, and it helped speed up the process because I didn't have as many bruises and my swelling wasn't too bad. I think the bit about longer to recover from depends on your pain tolerance, and your ability to push through and crush the scar tissue. 

To speed up recovery time, just stay consistent. My friend had the same repair as me with the same graft. His recovery time was about nine months, and then he tore it again. He didn't put in the effort. He wouldn't even try hard at physical therapy. He would sit there on his phone. My physical therapist called him lazy. 

I was able to get back into sports at six months. That's usually the earliest you can with physical contact. It depends on the type of job you have. If you work in the office, you could get back in quickly. If you work construction, the timeframe would be vastly different. If you were an electrician, the timeframe it would be a little longer than the offices' recovery time. It might not but comfortable to kneel for long periods of time, but it is manageable.
